This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, postoperative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), non-articular rheumatic disease (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis), and fever of acute upper respiratory tract infection in children.

At a glance

Category

OTC medicine

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code 172806ATB have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 1/2 to 1.5 tablets (200 to 600 mg) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and may take up to a maximum of 3200 mg per day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30-40 mg per kg of body weight per day in 3 to 4 divided doses; for mild to moderate pain or a cold, adults take 1/2 to 1 tablet (200 to 400 mg) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. For children aged 11 to 14 years, 200 to 250 mg per dose; aged 7 to 10 years, 150 to 200 mg per dose; aged 3 to 6 years, 100 to 150 mg per dose; aged 1 to 2 years, 50 to 100 mg per dose, administered orally 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg, the daily amount should not exceed 500 mg, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. Do not take more than the recommended dose. In the case of suppositories, for children insert 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight per dose deep into the rectum, 2 times a day. The dose may be adjusted appropriately according to age and symptoms.

Warning

  • If you regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day, consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.
  • Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, or cerebrovascular disease should avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day); patients with cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine if high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) is required.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine; patients with or with a history of gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood disorders, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe hypertension, or bronchial asthma; patients with or with a history of hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (including COX-2 inhibitors); patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass surgery; pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy; patients taking high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy; and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood disorders or a history thereof, patients with a bleeding tendency, cirrhosis, hepatic impairment or a history thereof, renal impairment or a history thereof, cardiac insufficiency or heart disease, hypertension, a history of hypersensitivity reactions, systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, the elderly and children, pregnant women, and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take this medicine in excess of the recommended dose.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock symptoms (heartburn, chills, dyspnea, low blood pressure), blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit and hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, decreased granulocytes, white blood cells, and platelets, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and increased eosinophils; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stool, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, diarrhea, gastric discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcer, constipation, melena; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reaction, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome), angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatic dysfunction such as hepatitis, jaundice, and elevation of GOT, GPT, ALP, hepatic impairment, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura (purple spots), rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, dyspnea or wheezing, visual disturbances such as scotoma, hearing loss (deafness), tinnitus, dysgeusia, dizziness, drowsiness, vertigo, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), low blood pressure, elevated blood pressure, palpitations (throbbing), heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina, acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urination), hematuria, proteinuria, elevation of BUN and serum creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, lethargy, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, peripheral edema, and Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency.

Interactions

  • Do not take it together with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, low-dose aspirin, or methotrexate.
  • When taken together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to take it

Adults and children aged 6 years or older take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day before bedtime; patients sensitive to adverse reactions take 1/2 tablet (5 mg) each in the morning and evening in divided doses. The dose may be adjusted appropriately according to age and symptoms. The dosing interval in patients with renal impairment must be adjusted according to the patient's renal function, and in pediatric patients with renal impairment the dose must be individually adjusted taking into account the patient's renal clearance and body weight, so refer to the approved labeling for details.

At a glance

How to take it

Adults take 1 to 2 tablets (125 to 250 mg) per dose 3 times a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with peptic ulcer, patients in whom drug-induced disturbance of the stomach or duodenum has occurred, patients hypersensitive to this drug, those who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, and patients with severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe heart failure, or inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis must not take this drug.
  • Before taking this medicine, those with a history of peptic ulcer, children and the elderly, patients with hypertension, fluid retention or heart failure, or bronchial asthma, and patients with or with a history of hepatic or renal impairment should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer and perforation, and rarely shock, rash, itching, anemia, elevation of AST and ALT, drowsiness, headache, dizziness, cold sweats, chills, or abnormal euphoria occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists, aspirin, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), cyclosporine and tacrolimus, antiplatelet agents and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), or corticosteroids.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients who are also being treated for peptic ulcer with misoprostol or a similar agent should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for nourishment and tonic effects, weak constitution, physical fatigue, febrile wasting diseases during or after illness, and nutritional supplementation during pregnancy/lactation, etc.

At a glance

Category

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code C36300ACH have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

Children aged 15 years or older and adults take 2 capsules per dose, 1 to 2 times a day.

Warning

  • Taking 5,000 IU or more of vitamin A a day may cause congenital malformations.
  • Women within the first 3 months of pregnancy or who may be pregnant should not take this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this drug, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with hypercalcemia (a condition in which calcium is present in excess in the blood), sarcoidosis (a systemic inflammatory disease of unknown cause), or renal disease must not take this drug.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants under 12 months of age, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and lactating women, patients with hyperoxaluria (a condition in which excessive amounts of oxalate are excreted in the urine), patients with a thrombotic predisposition, and patients deficient in folic acid should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms or if they worsen even after taking it for about 1 month, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It may interfere with the detection of glucose in various urine tests, and may turn the urine yellow, affecting clinical test values.

Possible side effects

  • If nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, itching, dry and rough skin, painful joint swelling, loose stools, gastric distension, abdominal discomfort, constipation, rash, redness, loss of appetite, or menstruation coming earlier than scheduled or the amount gradually increasing and bleeding lasting for a long time appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with levodopa.
  • When taken together with estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

At a glance

Category

Why this one

How to take it

Adults and children aged 12 years or older take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day. Children aged 6 to under 12 years take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day if they weigh 30 kg or more, and 1/2 tablet (5 mg) once a day if they weigh 30 kg or less.   • Before taking this medicine, patients with hepatic impairment or renal failure should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take it together with cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, quinidine, fluconazole, fluoxetine, or drugs that inhibit hepatic metabolism.

Adults and children aged 12 years or older take 1 to 1.5 g per dose 3 times a day, 30 minutes to 1 hour after meals. If necessary, one additional dose may be taken before bedtime.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, and patients with Alzheimer's disease, hemorrhoids, fluid retention (swelling), toxemia of pregnancy, diarrhea, or undiagnosed gastrointestinal bleeding should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with renal impairment, physically weak persons, those on a low-phosphorus diet, persons with impaired digestion and absorption, the elderly, patients with symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding such as hematemesis or black stools, and pregnant women, women who may be pregnant, and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving this medicine to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking this medicine for about 2 weeks, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If constipation, diarrhea, or similar symptoms appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take tetracycline antibiotics while taking this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, anti-ulcer agents, digitalis preparations, chlorpromazine, lansoprazole, prednisolone, penicillin, quinolones, iron (Fe) salt preparations, or salicylates should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

For chronic renal failure and osteoporosis, adults take 1 to 2 capsules (0.5 to 1 µg) once a day; for hypoparathyroidism and other diseases due to abnormal vitamin D metabolism, take 2 to 8 capsules (1 to 4 µg) once a day. For osteoporosis, children take 0.01 to 0.03 µg per kg of body weight once a day; for other diseases, take 0.05 to 0.1 µg per kg of body weight once a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this drug, patients with hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypermagnesemia, a Ca×P product > 3.7 (mmol/L)2, alkalemia with blood pH > 7.44 (milk-alkali syndrome, Burnett's syndrome), or signs of vitamin D toxicity must not take this drug.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and lactating women, children, the elderly, those with a history of renal stones, patients with sarcoidosis, and patients with hypersensitivity to Yellow No. 5 or those with a history thereof should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Follow the instructions regarding calcium intake as a dietary supplement or supplement.

Possible side effects

  • If occasionally anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, gastric pain and other gastrointestinal disorders, gastric discomfort, abdominal distension, indigestion, rarely dry mouth (thirst), oral paresthesia, polydipsia, pancreatitis, metallic taste, leg muscle cramps, headache, heavy-headedness, insomnia, irritability, asthenia, malaise, dizziness, numbness, drowsiness, heartburn, shoulder stiffness, senile hearing loss, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), decline in memory and recall, overt psychosis, disturbance of consciousness, back pain, mild blood pressure elevation, palpitations (pounding heart), cardiac arrhythmia, acute renal failure, elevated BUN and creatinine (decreased renal function), kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, hepatic dysfunction, jaundice, itching, rash, sensation of heat, conjunctival congestion, other conjunctivitis, corneal calcification, photophobia, periarticular calcification (heterotopic ossification), bone pain, hoarse voice, edema (swelling), weight loss, dysuria, polyuria (excessive urination), nocturia, ectopic calcification, muscle pain, runny nose, high fever, decreased libido, proteinuria, or hypercholesterolemia occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take magnesium-containing preparations, vitamin D and its derivatives, calcium-containing preparations, or thiazide diuretics.
  • Patients who are taking digitalis, resins such as cholestyramine, mineral oil which is a laxative, phenytoin and glucocorticoids, colestipol, sucralfate or antacids containing large amounts of aluminum, estrogens (ethinylestradiol, norethisterone), barbiturates, or antiepileptics should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
